tier_reason: The paper measures 4-lanes SHA-256 against OpenSSL 1.0.1c on an i7-3770 (Figs. 1-3: 12.78-13.27 vs 5.05-6.75 cycles/byte, 1.97-2.53x). It was peer-review published as Journal of Information Security 4(1):7-11, 2013 (DOI 10.4236/jis.2013.41002), with the same abstract numbers. There is no public code and no compiler or flags, so it is not A.

corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (3rd Gen Core, Ivy Bridge, AVX), with Hyper-Threading, Turbo Boost and Enhanced SpeedStep disabled
corrections.claimed_speedup: 4-lanes SHA-256 is 1.97-2.53x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1c for 2KB-128KB messages (Fig. 3: 13.27 vs 6.75 c/B at 2KB; 12.78 vs 5.05 c/B at 128KB). The abstract gives ~2 to ~2.5x. Against the fastest serial implementation (the authors' own n-SMS) it is 1.5-1.97x per the abstract and 1.55-2x per Sec. 3. At 8KB it is also faster than tree-mode BLAKE and Keccak (Fig. 4).
corrections.caveats: j-lanes SHA-256 is a different hash construction: a tree mode whose digest differs from standard SHA-256, and the paper itself says it would need distinct IVs if standardized. It is not a drop-in replacement for OpenSSL SHA-256. The 'fastest publicly available' comparator is the author's own n-SMS code. No compiler or flags are stated and no code is released. The results are from 2012 hardware against OpenSSL 1.0.1c, which predates OpenSSL's AVX2 and SHA-NI SHA-256 paths. The peer-reviewed venue is a SCIRP journal, a publisher whose review standards are widely questioned.

notes: The claimed numbers check out against both the ePrint PDF and the JIS 2013 abstract. The main issue for enrichment is that j-lanes changes the digest, so this is a new hash mode, not a faster SHA-256. B rests on the JIS (SCIRP) publication; if the orchestrator does not count SCIRP as peer review, it drops to C.

tier_reason: The paper benchmarks 4-buffer S-HASH SHA-256 against serial OpenSSL 1.0.1 on a Core i5-2500 (Fig. 2: 17.72-17.80 vs 5.18-5.21 c/B, i.e. 3.42x; Figs. 3-4 for disk). It was peer-review published as Journal of Information Security 3(4):319-325, 2012 (DOI 10.4236/jis.2012.34039). There is no code and no compiler or flags, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: From L1/L2/LLC/memory (4KB messages): 5.18-5.21 c/B vs OpenSSL 1.0.1 at 17.72-17.80 c/B, 3.42x, and 2.25x vs the authors' own n-SMS serial code. From disk at the native 3.3GHz: 2.26x (UNIFORM directory, 8.65 vs 19.55 c/B) and 1.73x (DIVERSE directory). The abstract's '~6.73 c/B, almost 3x' figure is with the CPU down-clocked to 1.6GHz (UNIFORM: 6.73 vs 19.26 c/B, 2.86x).
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i5-2500 (Sandy Bridge, 3.3GHz; some disk runs down-clocked to 2.6/1.7/1.6GHz), Turbo Boost, Hyper-Threading and SpeedStep disabled, 8GB DDR3-1600, RAID0 of two Intel SSD 320, Fedora 16
corrections.caveats: Applies only when many independent messages are available: each message still gets a standard SHA-256 digest, but a single message is not sped up (see j-lanes for that). OpenSSL RT ticket 2784 is the authors' n-SMS patch (the faster serial comparator), not S-HASH itself. No S-HASH code is released and no compiler or flags are stated. The disk results are bound by the SSDs, and the ~3x disk figure needs a down-clocked CPU. OpenSSL later shipped its own multi-buffer SHA-256 (crypto/sha/asm/sha256-mb-x86_64.pl, Polyakov, (c) 2013, used for multi-block AES-CBC-HMAC), so the incumbent absorbed the technique for that use. The results are from 2012 hardware against OpenSSL 1.0.1. The peer-reviewed venue is a SCIRP journal.

notes: The record's '~3x from disk at 6.73 c/B' omitted that this is at a 1.6GHz down-clock; at native frequency it is 2.26x. I rewrote the claim with the full numbers, and the tier stands. The RT 2784 caveat was misattributed and is fixed. B rests on the JIS (SCIRP) publication, and without it this would be C.

tier_reason: The README benchcmp tables are first-party. The only direct comparison with Go crypto/sha256 is the ARM64 table (Pine64 Cortex-A53); the x86 AVX512 and SHA-Ext figures are against the package's own AVX2 path. The benchmark code is public (sha256_test.go BenchmarkHash, which now includes a GoStdlib comparator), but no Go version or flags are given, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Against Go crypto/sha256 (the README's 'golang' column), the ARM64 path on a 1.2GHz Cortex-A53 (Pine64) is 8.38x at 8B, 57.75x at 1KB, 95.11x at 8KB and 105.49x at 1MB (638.23 vs 6.05 MB/s). That Go version predates stdlib ARM64 SHA2 support. The x86 figures are package-internal: AVX512 3498.20 vs its own AVX2 path 448.62 MB/s (7.80x, BenchmarkHash5M, 3.0GHz Xeon Platinum 8124M), and SHA Extensions 1975.17 vs its own AVX2 path 514.40 MB/s (3.84x, BenchmarkHash5M, 3.7GHz Ryzen 7 2700X per the README Performance table).
corrections.hardware: 3.0 GHz Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M (AVX512); 3.7 GHz AMD Ryzen 7 2700X (SHA Extensions); 1.2 GHz ARM Cortex-A53 (Pine64). The Celeron J3455 is only named as a SHA-Ext-capable CPU, not as a benchmark host.
corrections.workload: Single-core SHA256 hashing of 8B-10MB buffers (the Performance table uses >1MB blocks): the package's ARM64 path against Go crypto/sha256 on a Cortex-A53, and its AVX512 and SHA-Ext paths against its own AVX2 path on x86.
corrections.caveats: The Go stdlib has since caught up. crypto/sha256 gained an optimized arm64 (SHA2-instruction) implementation in a 2017-11-14 commit and a SHA-NI amd64 implementation in a 2023-03-31 commit. Issue #76 (Dec 2025) shows Go 1.25.5 stdlib matching or slightly beating the package's ARM path on an Apple M1 Max. The remaining edge is the AVX512 16-lane multi-buffer path, which is ported from Intel intel-ipsec-mb, needs an explicit Avx512Server and many concurrent goroutines, and is slower for messages under 1MB. It was never benchmarked against modern stdlib SHA-NI. The x86 README numbers are against the package's own AVX2 path, not the stdlib. No commits since 2023-02-22 (about 3.6 years), so it is flagged abandoned.

notes: Metadata verified: Apache-2.0, not archived, not a fork, 1,040 stars, last commit 2023-02-22, so abandoned is correct. The headline x86 speedups are not against the baseline, so I rewrote the claim to lead with the real stdlib comparison (ARM64) and to flag that the stdlib has since overtaken it. The tier stays C.
